document_title: Alaska's Half Vote and a Federal Bill
post_copy:
"The Ratepayer Protection Act will ensure that data centers pay their own way, instead of passing costs onto hardworking families."

Energy and Commerce Chairman Brett Guthrie said that when his committee advanced H.R. 9340 by 52 to 0. The bill never writes "data center". It describes one, a customer with 100 megawatts or more of peak demand who would pay the full incremental cost of the grid built to serve it.

A state whose legislature already voted on a comparable standard would be excused. Alaska's Senate passed SB 250 on May 16th, per Davis Wright Tremaine. No House floor vote appears in the public record.

A field labeled DATE OF ENACTMENT stays bare on all nine frames, because the bill is reported and on no published schedule.

The Department of Energy's record closes October 9th. What would Alaska's line in that record have to admit?

#DataCenterPolicy #LargeLoadCustomer #SB250

aftercare: Post it Tuesday to Thursday, 8 to 11 a.m. Alaska time. Drafts land daily and the cadence is the human's call, so hold this one for the next strong slot rather than pushing it into a Friday afternoon.
Paste the sources block as the first comment within 60 seconds of posting. No slide prints a source note, so until that comment lands the claims have no visible provenance.
Reply to every comment in the first 90 minutes, as the analyst and not as a brand account.
At 48 hours, write the saves and the comment count into the run record. Slide 08 is the keepable frame and saves are the honest test of whether it earned the keep.

If a commenter says the Alaska House voted SB 250 down, reply. No House floor vote appears in the record at all. It passed the Senate on May 16th, went to House Community and Regional Affairs, and died there, per Davis Wright Tremaine and BillTrack50.

If a commenter says Alaska is already exempt, reply. That may well be right. One of the three doors is a state commission proceeding, which needs no legislature, and nothing reachable says whether the Regulatory Commission of Alaska has run one. That gap is why the deck asks the question instead of answering it.

If a commenter says the bill is headed to the floor, reply. It sits on the Union Calendar, which makes it eligible for floor action. The Clerk's schedule and the majority leader's schedule were both read on September 13th and neither one lists it.

If a commenter sets the DeepGreen Cook Inlet figure beside the 100 megawatt threshold, reply. The FERC notice describes annual generation, which is energy, and the bill's threshold is peak demand, which is power. Same numeral, different quantity.
editor_notes_for_email:
WHAT THE DECK CLAIMS. H.R. 9340, the Ratepayer Protection Act, was reported to the House on September 10th as Report 119-814 and sits on the Union Calendar as number 713. It would make a customer with peak demand of 100 megawatts or more at a single site or campus pay the full incremental cost of any generation, transmission or distribution upgrade built to serve it, and that obligation survives the customer walking away from its contract. A state is excused if it already implemented a comparable standard, already conducted a proceeding on one, or its legislature already voted on one. Alaska's Senate passed SB 250 on May 16th and no House floor vote appears in the record. Whether one chamber satisfies "the State legislature has voted" is the deck's question and it is left as a question.

WHAT IT DELIBERATELY DOES NOT CLAIM. It never says Alaska is in or out of the exemption. It never says scheduled about this bill, only eligible for floor action. It puts no calendar date on the one year or two year clocks, because both run from an enactment that has not happened. Nothing about Begich, Sullivan or Murkowski, no cosponsor count, nothing about Gov. Dunleavy and the pledge, and nothing in either direction about what the Regulatory Commission of Alaska has or has not done. It never says the House voted SB 250 down. It never pairs the DeepGreen Cook Inlet 100 megawatt figure with the threshold, because that figure is annual energy and the threshold is peak power.

WHAT COULD DRAW A CORRECTION. Every SB 250 fact is secondary. akleg.gov refuses an automated read, so May 16th rests on Davis Wright Tremaine's energy practice and BillTrack50 agreeing, and both are named in type on slides 01 and 06. A reader holding the House journal could add detail there, which is the likeliest reply and a good one to get. The second exposure is prong two, the commission proceeding, which is genuinely unknown in both directions and is why the close is a question.

THE PIXEL ROOM AND WHAT IT CHANGED. Five critics read the nine frames and none of them said ship. The round that followed forced every display headline to break at its sense boundary rather than wherever the fitter landed, restored three body sentences the build had dropped from the plan, put the deck's DATE OF ENACTMENT motif back on the frames that had lost it, turned the closing frame's gold dates from raised glowing plaques into marks struck INTO the pad, and corrected two objects that were lit from the wrong side. All of it is recorded, per slide and with the reason, in the run's BUILD RECONCILIATION.

THE CAPTION. Carried byte for byte from the caption room's winner, hashtags included, at 898 chars with a 131 char hook. Checked against claims.json line by line and no factual error was found in it.
